launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Sunday from Florida, sending a new $4 billion observatory toward deep-space operations aimed at tackling dark energy, dark matter, and exoplanets. The mission matters because Roman is built to scan huge swaths of sky quickly, giving scientists a wide-field complement to existing space telescopes.

NASA officials described Roman as a major step up in survey speed versus older instruments, while maintaining image quality comparable to the Hubble Space Telescope.
At a July briefing, Roman senior project scientist
Julie McEnery
said the telescope can map the Milky Way in a month, adding, “One month of observations to survey our Milky Way galaxy would take about a century with Hubble," according to the report.
Nancy Grace Roman: Revolutionizing Space Observation

Roman is designed to extend the work of the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, and the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, by focusing on panoramic sky coverage rather than ultra-deep narrow views. NASA has compared that division of labor to wide-angle photography versus zoomed-in imaging.
Speaking to reporters Saturday, NASA Science Mission Directorate chief
Nicola Fox

framed the difference in blunt terms. "It will be ⁠as if Hubble and James Webb kind of peered through a keyhole at the universe, while Nancy Grace Roman will kick the door down,” Fox said, according to a report by Reuters.

What Breakthroughs Are Expected From Roman

One of Roman’s central goals is to help pin down what is driving the universe’s accelerating expansion, a phenomenon scientists reported in 1998 and often link to dark energy. Roman is also intended to measure how dark matter shapes cosmic structures through gravity over enormous distances.

Its flagship survey is expected to run for more than a year and chart more than two billion galaxies in three dimensions. NASA has said those measurements should let researchers compare dark matter’s gravitational effects with dark energy’s influence on expansion.
Roman also has a major planet-hunting role, with NASA expecting it to find thousands of worlds beyond our solar system and assemble a statistical picture of planetary systems that resemble our own.
How Roman Will Map The Universe Like Never Before
NASA says Roman’s wide-field approach is meant to pair with Webb’s ability to look far back in time, since distant light takes billions of years to reach Earth.
McEnery told reporters Webb is built to search for rare objects in the early universe, while Roman provides, “the large vision that complements the deep views that Webb provides.”
